questions.stem: A student investigates the effect of temperature on amylase activity by measuring how quickly starch disappears. At 60 degrees C, the starch is not broken down at all. What has happened to the amylase?

options.text: The amylase has been used up
The amylase has been denatured -- its active site shape has changed permanently
The starch concentration is too high
The amylase is working too quickly to measure

questions.explanation: At temperatures significantly above the optimum (typically around 37 degrees C for human enzymes), the enzyme is denatured. The heat breaks weak bonds holding the tertiary structure, changing the active site shape so the substrate (starch) can no longer fit. This is a permanent change -- the enzyme cannot recover its shape.

questions.stem: The lock-and-key model describes enzyme action. In this model, what does the 'lock' represent?

options.text: The substrate
The product
The active site of the enzyme
The enzyme inhibitor

questions.explanation: In the lock-and-key model, the active site (lock) has a specific shape that is complementary to the substrate (key). Only the correct substrate can fit into the active site, just as only the right key fits a specific lock. This explains enzyme specificity -- each enzyme works on only one type of substrate.

questions.stem: A graph shows that enzyme activity increases as substrate concentration increases, then levels off to a plateau. What causes the plateau?

options.text: The enzyme has been denatured by excess substrate
All the enzyme active sites are occupied (saturated) so adding more substrate has no effect
The products are inhibiting the reaction
The temperature has changed

questions.explanation: At the plateau, every enzyme active site is continuously occupied by substrate molecules (enzyme saturation). Even though more substrate is available, there are no free active sites for it to bind to. The rate can only increase further by adding more enzyme molecules.

questions.stem: Biological washing powders contain proteases and lipases. Why do they work better at 30-40 degrees C than at 90 degrees C?

options.text: Lower temperatures clean clothes more effectively
The enzymes work near their optimum temperature at 30-40 degrees C but would be denatured at 90 degrees C
The enzymes need cold water to dissolve
Hot water destroys the fabric of clothes

questions.explanation: The enzymes in biological washing powders have an optimum temperature of around 30-40 degrees C. At this temperature, they effectively break down protein and fat stains. At 90 degrees C, the enzymes would be denatured, losing their function. This is also why biological powders save energy compared to hot washes.

questions.stem: Pepsin works in the stomach (pH 2) and trypsin works in the small intestine (pH 8). If trypsin were placed in the stomach, what would happen?

options.text: Trypsin would work faster due to the high acid concentration
Trypsin would be denatured because the pH is far from its optimum
Trypsin would convert to pepsin
Trypsin would have no effect at any pH

questions.explanation: Each enzyme has an optimum pH at which it works best. Extreme changes in pH alter the charges on amino acids in the active site, disrupting the bonds that maintain its shape. Trypsin's active site would be denatured at pH 2, preventing it from binding to its substrate. This is why different enzymes work in different parts of the digestive system.
